headline: Iowa to drop hemp products over federal THC cap from its state list
dek: Iowa HHS says products above the 0.4 mg per-container federal limit lose their place on its Master Product List from 11 December, with no sell-through period.
key_points: Iowa's health department says hemp products that exceed the new federal limits will be removed automatically from the state's Master Product List and refused for compliance review.
Iowa's own limits of 4 mg THC per serving and 10 mg per container stay on the books, but the state's container cap is 25 times the federal 0.4 mg ceiling that applies from 11 December.
There is no sell-through period and no refund of registration fees, and some full-spectrum CBD products may also fall foul of the federal cap.
West Virginia's agriculture commissioner, Kent Leonhardt, is urging Congress to regulate rather than ban, citing his state's 1,000-plus registered retailers and 611 seized illegal products.
body: Iowa will not wait for federal agents to clear its shelves. The state's Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has published guidance saying that hemp products exceeding the new federal THC limits will be removed automatically from Iowa's Master Product List, the register of products cleared for sale, and that new submissions over the federal line will no longer be accepted for review. The Marijuana Herald reported the guidance on 16 November.

The practical effect is that a product Iowa approved last month can lose its state listing on 11 December without anyone touching the state's law. Iowa's own THC limits stay exactly as they are; the department simply says its hemp rules cannot be applied in conflict with federal law.
## Two federal dates, one state list

The federal change comes from the hemp provision in the funding law signed in November 2025, which redefines hemp using total THC, including THCA, and caps finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products at 0.4 milligrams of THC and similar cannabinoids per container. Iowa HHS lists two start dates. From 12 November 2026, cannabinoids that cannot be naturally produced by the cannabis plant no longer count as hemp. From 11 December 2026, the 0.4 mg container limit and total-THC rules take effect, after Congress delayed most of the change by a month.

Iowa's rules allow up to 4 mg of THC per serving and 10 mg per container. HHS gives a simple example: a drink with 4 mg of THC meets Iowa's limit but is ten times over the federal one. By MetaFlora's arithmetic, Iowa's maximum container is 25 times the federal cap, which means almost every intoxicating hemp product the state has registered will drop off the list on 11 December.
> Iowa built one of the tighter hemp regimes in the country. On 11 December its strictest legal product becomes 25 times too strong.

The guidance is blunt about inventory. Federal law has no general sell-through period, HHS says, so registrants should review stock now and arrange returns with suppliers before the deadline. Products that cannot be returned should be disposed of lawfully, if necessary with local law enforcement, and the department says it has no power to direct how controlled substances are destroyed.

Products over the federal limit may become Schedule I controlled substances, the department warns, and an Iowa registration does not authorise selling a product that federal law prohibits. The Herald adds that businesses will not get refunds or prorated credits on registration fees already paid, even if they have to close.

Non-intoxicating products are not automatically safe either. HHS says some CBD products, including full-spectrum CBD with trace THC, may exceed the per-container limit, because the cap applies to the whole container rather than per serving. Registrants are told to check their formulas and certificates of analysis. Products that meet both federal and Iowa rules stay on the list without resubmission, and the department says it will notify registrants if Congress changes or delays the rules.
## West Virginia argues for a different path

Iowa's approach is to comply. West Virginia's agriculture commissioner wants Congress to change course. In an op-ed published on 13 November, Kent Leonhardt argued that 11 December will reclassify many CBD oils and hemp products that West Virginians use every day, and that his state's system shows they can be regulated instead.

West Virginia has licensed hemp product makers and sellers since 2023, with contaminant and potency testing, labelling standards and a 21-and-over limit on intoxicating products. Leonhardt wrote that more than 1,000 retail locations registered with his department in 2024, and that inspectors ran 276 inspections in 45 counties and confiscated 611 illegal products that year. The state has also halved its product registration fee, to $100 from $200, for hemp grown, harvested and made in West Virginia, the Herald reported.

He asks Congress to set national standards for independent lab testing, accurate labels, potency limits and age limits, to let states go further, and to delay the deadline again so a framework can be written. He also notes that the synthetic-cannabinoid restriction, which he calls a legitimate concern, has already taken effect.

Time is short. As we reported this morning, Rep. James Comer (R-KY) told Kentucky hemp businesses that a stand-alone hemp bill is unlikely to get a vote, and that attaching protections to the next stopgap funding bill is the best chance. Government funding also runs out on 11 December, so the hemp deadline and the spending fight now share a date.

From today there are 25 days until 11 December. Watch the next continuing resolution for any hemp language, Iowa HHS notices to registrants if federal rules shift, and similar product-list purges in other states that run hemp registries. A federal court in Illinois hears a challenge to that state's hemp THC limits on 19 November, another sign of how many fronts this fight is now on.
